101.0.0.en: I will sing of mercy and judgment: unto thee, O LORD, will I sing.

101.0.1.en: 1- Divine mercy precedes God’s judgment and condemnation, for God wants everyone to be saved. For this reason David sings and chants that mercy precedes judgment; indeed, God is merciful in His judgment, as He stopped the plague with which God punished David for numbering the people (2 Sam 24:15, 16). And God is also wise in His mercy, for He allowed the child born of the adultery of David and the wife of Uriah the Hittite to fall sick, that David might know that the result of adultery is hateful to God; He forgave David, but the child died (2 Sam 12:13-15).

101.0.2.en: 2- God’s mercy is in this life, to give us an opportunity to repent, while judgment is on the last day of judgment.

101.0.3.en: 3- God’s mercies are many, and it is natural for David to sing of them, but the wonder is that he also sings of God’s judgment and justice. He sings of the justice of God that would be accomplished in the fullness of time, when Christ paid the debt owed by mankind on the Cross. And David sings of God’s judgment and condemnation by which He punishes the demons and destroys them in eternal torment.

101.0.4.en: 4- If God’s mercy precedes His judgment, then the children of God ought to let mercy precede judgment in their feelings and their deeds toward others, so that they seek the salvation of everyone’s souls like God.

101.1.0.en: I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.

101.1.1.en: 1- David declares his course in life by his promise to God that he will walk in perfection and with wisdom; that is, he will understand all that he does, and be exact in it, and walk according to the commandments of God. And he walked in perfection not only before men but also in the midst of his house, in dealing with his family and his servants, and in all his personal affairs. And his walking in perfection comes from his heart, and is not outward, superficial behavior.

101.1.3.en: 2- When David mentioned his striving to walk in perfection he remembered his weakness and shortcoming, so he asked God to come to him, to support him in carrying out His commandments. He also entreats God, declaring his longing that He come to him and bless him, as He promised Moses of old (Ex 20:24). And likewise his asking that God come is a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ to redeem mankind.

101.2.0.en: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.

101.2.1.en: On the path of perfection David declares that he does not set before his eyes as a goal any wicked thing, because he hates it and does not want to cleave to it. Although as a human being he is liable to fall into any sin, he does not set sin as the goal of his life, but keeps away from it and hates it, because he wants to cleave to God and walk in His commandments.

101.2.2.en: Set God as your goal at the beginning of your day, that you may hold fast to His commandments, and please Him in your thoughts, your words and your deeds, and keep away from evil, even if everyone around you walks in his own way, and remain cleaving to God, and you will always enjoy your peace.

101.2.3.en: (2) Keeping away from the wicked and cleaving to the faithful (vv. 4-8:)

101.3.0.en: A froward heart shall depart from me: I will not know a wicked person.

101.3.1.en: David continues his speech about perfection, and affirms that he keeps away from the crooked, that is, those whose hearts are twisted away from God, and from all the wicked. He does not want to mix with evil lest he fall into it, and this shows his exactness and his purity. In this he is a symbol of Christ the righteous and holy, who is repelled by evil.

101.4.0.en: Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer.

101.4.1.en: “Slandereth”: judges another in his absence. David adds to his pure conduct that he keeps away from the wicked who commit two great sins:

101.4.2.en: 1- Judging and slander: because they are against love of the other, and also wound him, and are a stumbling block to the hearers, and the loss of peace of the one who judges; so it is an evil from every side, with many offenses.

101.4.3.en: 2- Pride: whether in the heart, or in conduct by the look, or in speech, or in behavior.

101.4.4.en: So David the prophet could not bear these two sins, and he shunned anyone who walked in them.

101.5.0.en: Mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me.

101.5.1.en: In order that King David might keep away from injustice in his judgments and decisions, he shunned the wicked, and at the same time brought near to himself those faithful to God and those who walk in perfection. For the just ruler is not content only to shun the wicked, but must surround himself with the faithful and the perfect, as David befriended Jonathan, and as Christ drew near to Himself the twelve disciples and the seventy Apostles, and loved Lazarus and his two sisters Mary and Martha.

101.6.0.en: He that worketh deceit shall not dwell within my house: he that telleth lies shall not tarry in my sight.

101.6.1.en: 1- David continues his speech about the purity of the atmosphere around him, and declares that whoever acts with deceit or lies does not settle inside his house. Even if the liar and the deceiver try to slip into David’s palace, he drives him out and does not let him settle with him in the house.

101.6.2.en: 2- If thoughts of deceit or lying try to enter the heart of the spiritual man, he rejects them and does not let them settle within him.

101.7.0.en: I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD.

101.7.1.en: 1- David concludes the psalm with his hatred of evil, so he destroys it from his city Jerusalem, and hastens to this by rising early to rid himself of evil, in order to preserve the purity of the city and of all who are around him.

101.7.2.en: 2- The city symbolizes the heart of the spiritual man, and the Church, which ought to remain pure, as St. Paul the Apostle did and separated the sinner in the church of Corinth until he repented (1 Cor 5:

101.7.3.en: Examine yourself every day so that you rid yourself of your sins by repentance, and indeed cut yourself off and keep away from the sources of evil, that you may live in peace and purity and enjoy fellowship with God.

101.7.4.en: The sufferings of the poor man and his hope. A prayer of the afflicted, when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD: “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and let my cry come unto thee … v. 1”

101.7.6.en: 1- Its author: there are several opinions on this matter:

101.7.7.en: a- The name of the psalm’s author is not mentioned in the title, so it is considered one of the orphan psalms, since it says that its author is a poor man and does not mention his name.

101.7.8.en: b- David the prophet, who was poor in spirit, that is, humble before God, and endured many pains, so he lifted up his prayer to God.

101.7.9.en: c- Ezra the priest and scribe wrote it at the end of the captivity, and it expresses the pains of the captives and their longing to return to Jerusalem.

101.7.10.en: d- Nehemiah, who returned from the captivity to Jerusalem in the third return, and saw the wall of Jerusalem broken down and the stones scattered, so he prayed and God supported him, and he built the wall and cared for Jerusalem and its inhabitants spiritually and materially.

101.7.13.en: a- When David was driven out from the face of Absalom his son.

101.7.14.en: b- At the end of the period of the captivity and the beginning of the return to Jerusalem.

101.7.15.en: 3- This psalm expresses the pains of the poor who believe in God and are humble before Him, and their hope in His salvation.

101.7.16.en: 4- In a large part of this psalm he speaks in the voice of the congregation, for it expresses the pains of the people of God and their supplication to Him to rescue them.

101.7.17.en: 5- This psalm is one of the messianic psalms, and this poor man symbolizes Christ, who endured sufferings for our sake and prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane that the cup of sufferings might pass from Him.

101.7.18.en: 6- This psalm is considered one of the liturgical psalms, for it was used in public worship, being offered as a prayer on the days of God.

101.7.19.en: 7- This psalm is considered one of the seven penitential psalms, which are (Ps 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143).

101.7.20.en: 8- St. Paul the Apostle quoted a part of this psalm, which is (vv. 25-27), in his Epistle to the Hebrews (ch. 1:10-12), and this confirms that the words of the psalm prophesy about Christ.

101.7.21.en: 9- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.

102.0.s.en: (1) The sufferings of the poor man

102.0.0.en: Hear my prayer, O LORD, and let my cry come unto thee. Hide not thy face from me in the day when I am in trouble; incline thine ear unto me: in the day when I call answer me speedily.

102.0.1.en: 1- The supplication of the psalmist shows his need of God, and he asks Him to hear his prayer, indeed that his cry, which expresses the extent of his need, enter into the presence of God. He does not cry with a loud voice, but rather his heart cries, because he is in great pain. And in the intensity of his need he entreats God not to hide His face from him or forget him. Indeed, he hopes that God will incline His ear and hear him, for he trusts in God’s love and humility. Although the voice of the poor man is low because of the intensity of the pains, his hope is that God will condescend, incline His ear, and listen to him. And because of his great need he wishes for God’s speedy answer.

102.0.2.en: 2- These two verses are a prophecy about the crucified Christ, from whom the face of the Father was hidden, so He cried “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mt 27:46) as an expression of the difficulty of bearing all the sins of the world, for He had to drink the cup of sufferings to the end and die to complete our redemption.

102.1.0.en: 3- For my days are consumed in smoke, and my bones are dried up like firewood. 4- My heart is scorched like grass and withered, so that I neglected to eat my bread. 5- By reason of the voice of my groaning my bone cleaveth to my flesh.

102.1.1.en: “Firewood”: the dry branches with which fire is kindled.

102.1.2.en: “Scorched”: a hot wind blew on it and made it dry.

102.1.4.en: The psalmist describes the effect of the pains on him, until they made his life like smoke that quickly scatters and ends; that is, his life is almost consumed by the intensity of the pain, and likewise his bones have become like sticks of firewood used to kindle a fire. The bones are the strong part in man that supports the body; these have become very weak and have begun to burn, and the bones that support man have been turned into a cause of fire being kindled within him, that is, the cause of his violent pains. Then he likens his life to a plant on which a hot wind has blown and made it dry.

102.1.5.en: And the scorched plant loses its vitality and becomes firewood for kindling fire, unless the divine waters come to its aid to water it and restore its vitality. So also the heart of the poor man dries up from the intensity of the pains. And in the end he no longer has ability or desire to eat food, but has forgotten it, and so has become liable to die of hunger; in addition, his sighing and constant groaning because of the intensity of the pains made his flesh cleave to his bones, since the whole body has become dry and liable to perish.

102.2.0.en: 6- I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am become like an owl of the ruins. 7- I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.

102.2.1.en: “Pelican of the wilderness”: a kind of bird, some of which live in the wilderness, and which makes sounds like the cry of one who suffers and mourns. It feeds on poisonous animals such as snakes.

102.2.2.en: “Owl of the ruins”: a kind of bird that makes sad sounds and lives in tombs and ruined places, and the Arabs consider it an omen of ill fortune.

102.2.4.en: 1- The psalmist likens his painful state to the birds that make sad sounds, such as the pelican and the owl. And because of the intensity of his pains he has kept away from loved ones and suffers from isolation; therefore he likens himself to a lone sparrow on the roof of a house, with no one with him and no one aware of him, especially since this sparrow means the house sparrow that stands alone on the roofs of houses in the cold weather.

102.2.5.en: 2- These two verses symbolize Christ, who trod the winepress alone and bore all the pains for us on the Cross, like the pelican and the owl, which are among the unclean, sorrowful birds, because He bore our uncleannesses and our sorrows, and He was alone in the sufferings and everyone left Him, so He was like the lone sparrow.

102.3.0.en: 8- Mine enemies reproach me all the day; and they that are mad against me are sworn against me.

102.3.2.en: “Are sworn against me”: have banded together against me; that is, they agreed to do me harm and swore to it.

102.3.3.en: 1- This poor man also endured reproaches from enemies, and many of those who were enraged at him because of his righteousness conspired against him. And they continued like this all the day; that is, they continually troubled him with hard words, and affirmed that they would do him harm.

102.3.4.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, who endured many reproaches from the Jews, and they were enraged at Him, and did Him harm by scourging and crucifixion.

102.4.0.en: 9- For I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping. The psalmist expresses the extent of his pains and his humiliation before God, for he put ashes on his head as was the custom of the ancients, and when he ate food the ashes fell from his head and mixed with his food; that is, he was in great austerity and humiliation. And when he drank water, or any other drink, in his intense sorrows, his tears would flow and fall into his drink, and he would drink his drink mixed with his tears. All this shows the extent of his pains.

102.5.0.en: 10- Because of thine indignation and thy wrath: for thou hast lifted me up, and cast me down.

102.5.1.en: All the pains that passed over the psalmist, he felt were by God’s permission. God was greatly angry with him, so He lifted him up and cast him down, and he suffered pains as a result of being thrown on the ground. And this shows the extent of his faith and his acceptance of the pains from the hand of God, for he felt that they were a discipline for him, that he might repent and renounce the world. And God raised David to the throne of the kingdom, but allowed his son to rise against him, who drove him out and tried to kill him, but when David prayed God restored him to his throne.

102.6.0.en: 11- My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass.

102.6.1.en: 1- The psalmist feels his weakness, and likens his life to a shadow that declines on the ground. This shadow grows longer the nearer the time of sunset, that is, man grows older, but after the sun disappears it vanishes completely, that is, life ends, so he sees that his life will end. And he also expresses his pains by saying that he is near perishing, so he likens himself to grass uprooted from its roots in the earth that has begun to dry, and so is near losing its vitality, that is, becoming firewood; such is the life of the psalmist.

102.6.2.en: 2- This verse applies to Christ, whose life on earth was short and ended with His crucifixion, and who endured all the pains out of love for us.

102.6.3.en: If you suffer pains, be faithful to God, holding fast to His commandments, and trust that your pains are very precious to God, and He will reward you for them in the Kingdom.

102.7.0.en: 12- But thou, O LORD, sittest for ever; and thy memorial unto all generations.

102.7.1.en: 1- The psalmist is a weak human being and his life is short, but God is great and glorified, sitting on His throne, and the heavenly ones remember Him, and His children on earth from generation to generation glorify His name. So although man is suffering and weak on earth, he will be made happy by seeing God and will glorify Him in the heavens. And this shows the psalmist’s faith in eternal life and its glories, and this helps him to bear the temporary pains of the earth.

102.7.2.en: 2- Though the life of Christ on earth was filled with pains and He died a terrible death by crucifixion, He is glorified in the heavens for ever and ever.

102.8.0.en: 13- Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come.

102.8.1.en: “Zion”: the most important of the five hills on which the city of Jerusalem stands, and it symbolizes the holy city.

102.8.2.en: 1- The psalmist shows his hope in the mighty God who sits for ever on His throne, who will have compassion at the set time when the times are fulfilled and bring His people back from captivity. He arises to help His people after they have endured discipline, to free them from their bondage and return them to their land, that they may build the Temple and worship Him in it; thereby fulfilling the words of the prophecies (Isa 40:2; Jer 29:10; Hab 2:3).

102.8.3.en: 2- This verse points to the redemption of Christ in the fullness of time, and His Resurrection, that He might raise His children in Him and save them from their sins.

102.8.4.en: 3- This verse also points to the final resurrection after the day of judgment, when He will have compassion on His believing children and compensate them for all their toils on earth.

102.9.0.en: 14- For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.

102.9.1.en: 1- The servants of God are the Jews who believe in God and hold fast to His worship, who went into captivity, but still long for the stones of the ruined Temple in Jerusalem, that they may build it anew. And they also yearned for the dust of Jerusalem to restore it to its former splendor, and by this they draw out God’s mercies and compassion, that He may help them to build the Temple and Jerusalem anew.

102.9.2.en: 2- In this verse the “servants of God” symbolize the Apostles who took pleasure in the stones of the Church, that is, the believers, and yearned for her dust, that is, for those who are far off and walk in an earthly, dusty way of life, to preach to them and draw them to the Church.

102.10.0.en: 15- So the heathen shall fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth thy glory.

102.10.1.en: When the Gentiles see God’s care for His people in bringing them back from captivity and helping them to build the Temple and Jerusalem, they believe in the power of God, the God of Israel, and fear Him, they and their kings, and indeed turn to faith, and this is what happened in Christianity when the Gentiles believed and became strong churches at the hands of the Apostles, especially St. Paul the Apostle.

102.11.0.en: 16- When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.

102.11.1.en: 1- The psalmist believed that Zion would be built, and so the glory of God who built it by means of His children who believe in Him would appear, and this great work draws the Gentiles to faith.

102.11.2.en: 2- God’s work in building up His believing children glorifies God, so many of those who are far off believe. This is what happens in the Church every day.

102.12.0.en: 17- He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.

102.12.1.en: Here the psalmist speaks in the past tense of God, that He regarded the prayer of the destitute, who is the believer in God who is in distress and has nothing before him but to take refuge in God, and He took heed of his petition and did not neglect it, and helped His captive children and brought them back to Jerusalem, and they built the Temple and the city. This shows the extent of the psalmist’s faith in the answer of God that will take place.

102.13.0.en: 18- This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.

102.13.1.en: In the spirit of prophecy the psalmist declares a great truth, that not only will the people of God return from the captivity and build the Temple again in Jerusalem, but a people will be created who will praise the Lord in the following generations, that is, the generation to come, and he means in the fullness of time when Christ redeems mankind and establishes His Church by His Holy Spirit, and she praises Him with a new praise, around a new sacrifice, which is the sacrifice of Himself (His Body and Blood.)

102.14.0.en: 19- For he hath looked down from the height of his sanctuary; from heaven did the LORD behold the earth; 20- To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to

102.14.1.en: loose those that are appointed to death; God the compassionate has been occupied since eternity with His children who fell into sin but who believe in Him and await His salvation, and in the fullness of time He looked down and beheld from heaven, that is, He cared for His children and showed His love toward them by His Incarnation and redemption, for He heard their groaning and their pain at the dominion of the devil over them, and the sentence of death that had been passed upon them, indeed their distress at hell, which they had entered, so He stretched out His hand and saved them, and raised them up to paradise, after He had completed their redemption on the Cross.

102.15.0.en: 21- To declare the name of the LORD in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem; 22- When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms, to serve the LORD.

102.15.1.en: After many in the whole world believed in Christ the Redeemer, they offered praises to God in Jerusalem, or the new Zion, that is, the Church. And the name of the Lord Jesus Christ was declared, and praises were offered to Him, when the peoples who believed in Him gathered around Him.

102.15.2.en: God is ready, however much you have sinned, to forgive your sins and rebuild your spiritual life, so you return and offer Him thanksgiving and praise, and enjoy not only your first fellowship with Him but also experience new depths in His love.

102.16.0.en: 23- He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days. 24- I said, O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days: thy years are for ever and ever.

102.16.1.en: “Weakened”: made weak, that is, made it feeble.

102.16.2.en: The psalmist expresses the pains he suffers as a human being, which make him weak, and he feels that his body is not strong enough to complete his days on earth; therefore he asks God to lengthen his days and not to let the pains shorten them, for he longs to see the salvation of God that would be accomplished in the fullness of time, which God promised by the mouth of the prophets, that is, the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption. And he says to God: You endure for ever, so lengthen my life and grant me to live before You, that I may see and enjoy this salvation. So it is clear that all the believers in the Old Testament longed for the salvation of Christ, as St. Paul the Apostle expressed this in his Epistle to the Hebrews by saying that they “saw them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them” (Heb 11:13), that is, they were longing for them.

102.17.0.en: 25- Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth: and the heavens are the work of thy hands. 26- They shall perish, but thou remainest: and they all shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed. 27- But thou art he, and thy years shall not end. 28- The children of thy servants shall dwell, and their seed shall be established before thee.

102.17.1.en: 1- In these verses the psalmist declares that God is the Eternal One who created heaven and earth and all that is in them. And that all the material things in the world will perish, but human beings God will change into spiritual bodies that will live forever with their spirits. And although material creatures perish, God their Creator endures forever, and with Him endure His children and servants who believe in Him, and all their descendants who lived a spiritual life like them with God. All these are immortal and enjoy the Kingdom of Heaven from God.

102.17.2.en: 2- And so we see that at the beginning of the psalm the author speaks of the pains that people experience, even believers in God, but he concludes the psalm with a great happiness that the children of God receive in return for all their toils on earth, because they believed in God and loved Him.

102.17.3.en: May your eyes be lifted to heaven every day, even for minutes, to remember that your only goal in this life is to reach heaven, so that you live with uprightness of heart and purity on this day, and keep away from what makes you stumble, and if you fall you return quickly in repentance to God, so that you keep your eyes raised toward heaven.

102.17.4.en: A call to all to praise the Lord: “Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name … v. 1”

102.17.6.en: 1- Its author: David the prophet, as the title of the psalm states.

102.17.7.en: 2- When was it written? At the end of David’s life, that is, in his old age, so he praises God and blesses Him with all his heart for His works with him and with his people.

102.17.8.en: 3- Some see this psalm as a prophecy of the praise and blessing of the people of God returning from the captivity.

102.17.9.en: 4- This psalm shows the feelings of David and his people toward God, while the next psalm (Ps 104) is similar to this psalm in praising God, and both end with the phrase “Bless the LORD, O my soul,” but the latter psalm expresses the praise of God by the whole creation.

102.17.10.en: 5- This psalm is a prophecy of the blessings of the awaited Messiah, so it is considered one of the messianic psalms.

102.17.11.en: 6- This psalm is liturgical; the Jews used to repeat it in the Temple, and they still worship with it to this day.

102.17.12.en: 7- This psalm suits everyone who loves God and wishes to thank Him, for it expresses strong feelings of love for God.

102.17.13.en: 8- This psalm is not found in the prayer of the Agpeya.
